title: Macbeth
question: Reread Lady Macbeth's line below. How does she use the idea of being "a man" to push Macbeth toward the murder? Support your answer with one detail from Scene 7. “When you durst do it, then you were a man”
model_answer: Lady Macbeth defines manhood as daring to act on what one wants, so Macbeth's hesitation becomes a loss of manhood. She reminds him that he was "a man" when he first proposed the plan and calls him a coward "in thine own esteem" who lets "I dare not" wait upon "I would." Macbeth replies that a true man knows limits ("Who dares do more is none"), but by the end of the scene he is "settled."
rubric_2: Explains that she links manhood to daring or acting on desire, so backing out makes him less of a man or a coward, AND supports it with a relevant detail from Scene 7 (the coward taunt, the cat proverb, the babe image, Macbeth's reply about what becomes a man, or his final "I am settled").
rubric_1: Says she insults or pressures him but does not explain the link between manhood and daring, OR gives an accurate reading with no supporting detail.
rubric_0: Misreads the line (for example, says she praises his restraint or means only courage in battle) or does not address it.
evidence: When you durst do it, then you were a man; And, to be more than what you were, you would Be so much more the man. … And live a coward in thine own esteem, Letting "I dare not" wait upon "I would," … I dare do all that may become a man; Who dares do more is none. … I am settled, and bend up Each corporal agent to this terrible feat.

title: Macbeth
question: Reread the Old Man's report below. What does this event in nature suggest about Duncan's murder? Support your answer with one other detail from Scene 4. “A falcon, towering in her pride of place, Was by a mousing owl hawk'd at and kill'd.”
model_answer: A noble falcon at the height of its flight is killed by an owl that normally hunts mice, which reverses the natural order just as a subject killing his king does. The Old Man himself calls it "unnatural, even like the deed that's done." Ross adds that Duncan's horses broke loose and ate each other and that darkness covers the earth in daytime, so nature itself seems thrown into disorder by the crime.
rubric_2: Explains that the lowly owl killing the high falcon mirrors a subject killing his king (or that nature is overturned by the murder), AND cites another relevant detail from Scene 4 (the horses, the daytime darkness, the Old Man's "unnatural" comment).
rubric_1: Gives a partly accurate reading (for example, says only that it is a bad omen) without linking it to the murder, OR gives an accurate reading with no supporting detail.
rubric_0: Misreads the image (for example, treats it as a literal hunting story with no connection to Duncan) or does not address it.
evidence: 'Tis unnatural, Even like the deed that's done. … And Duncan's horses (a thing most strange and certain) Beauteous and swift, the minions of their race, Turn'd wild in nature, broke their stalls, flung out, … by the clock 'tis day, And yet dark night strangles the travelling lamp.

title: Macbeth
question: Reread Lennox's remark below. What is Lennox really suggesting about who killed Banquo and Duncan? Support your answer with one other detail from Scene 6. “And the right valiant Banquo walk'd too late; Whom, you may say, if't please you, Fleance kill'd, For Fleance fled.”
model_answer: Lennox is speaking ironically: if fleeing proves guilt, then Fleance must have killed his own father, which is absurd, so the same logic cannot convict Duncan's sons either. He hints that Macbeth is the real killer. He also mocks Macbeth's "pious rage" in killing the grooms ("Was not that nobly done?") and openly calls Macbeth "the tyrant."
rubric_2: Recognizes the irony (Lennox does not believe Fleance or Duncan's sons are guilty and points toward Macbeth), AND supports it with another detail from Scene 6 (the mock praise of Macbeth's grief or of killing the grooms, the word "tyrant," the hope for help from England).
rubric_1: Senses that Lennox doubts the official story but does not identify Macbeth as the implied killer, OR gives an accurate reading with no supporting detail.
rubric_0: Takes Lennox literally (for example, says he believes Fleance killed Banquo) or does not address the passage.

title: Macbeth
question: Reread Macbeth's vow below, made when he hears that Macduff has fled to England. What does it suggest about how Macbeth will now act on his thoughts? Support your answer with one detail from Act 4. “From this moment The very firstlings of my heart shall be The firstlings of my hand.”
model_answer: Macbeth vows that from now on his first impulses (the "firstlings of my heart") will be carried out at once by his hand, with no pause for thought or conscience between wanting and doing. Having just missed Macduff, he decides that a purpose not acted on immediately is lost ("The flighty purpose never is o'ertook Unless the deed go with it"). He at once orders the surprise of Macduff's castle and the killing of "his wife, his babes," to be done "before this purpose cool," which shows how far he has moved from the man who hesitated before killing Duncan.
rubric_2: Explains that Macbeth will now turn his first impulses straight into action, with no delay or reflection between thought and deed, AND supports it with a relevant detail from Act 4 ("be it thought and done," the flighty purpose that must be overtaken by the deed, the planned attack on Macduff's wife and children, "before this purpose cool," or the murders at Fife in Scene 2).
rubric_1: Says Macbeth is growing more violent or wants to kill Macduff's family but does not explain the link between heart (thought) and hand (action), OR gives an accurate reading with no supporting detail.
rubric_0: Misreads the line (for example, says he vows to follow his heart's love, to think more carefully, or to stop killing) or does not address it.
evidence: Time, thou anticipat'st my dread exploits: The flighty purpose never is o'ertook Unless the deed go with it. … To crown my thoughts with acts, be it thought and done: The castle of Macduff I will surprise; Seize upon Fife; give to th' edge o' th' sword His wife, his babes, and all unfortunate souls That trace him in his line. … This deed I'll do before this purpose cool:

title: Macbeth
question: Reread Macbeth's words about the witches below. What has he come to understand about their prophecies? Support your answer with one Act 5 detail showing a prophecy fulfilled in an unexpected way. “That palter with us in a double sense; That keep the word of promise to our ear, And break it to our hope!”
model_answer: Macbeth realizes that the prophecies were double-edged: their words were literally true, but they misled him into false confidence. "None of woman born" sounded like no one at all, yet Macduff was "from his mother's womb untimely ripp'd." Likewise, Birnam Wood did come to Dunsinane, but only because Malcolm's soldiers carried boughs cut from it.
rubric_2: Explains that the prophecies were literally true but deceptive (they kept the promise "to our ear" but not "to our hope"), AND supports it with a specific Act 5 detail of a prophecy fulfilled unexpectedly (Macduff's birth, the soldiers carrying boughs from Birnam Wood, or the Messenger's report that the wood began to move).
rubric_1: Says the witches lied or tricked him without explaining the double meaning, OR gives an accurate reading with no supporting detail.
rubric_0: Misreads the passage (for example, says Macbeth still trusts the prophecies) or does not address it.
evidence: I pull in resolution; and begin To doubt th' equivocation of the fiend, That lies like truth. … Despair thy charm; And let the angel whom thou still hast serv'd Tell thee, Macduff was from his mother's womb Untimely ripp'd. … Let every soldier hew him down a bough, And bear't before him.
